answer: Each agent can submit a claim only after locking a scarce resource—such as a deposit or compute credits—and the protocol slashes that lock when independent audits find fabricated work. A sybil attacker must therefore fund every identity and risk losing its stake, rather than create unlimited costless accounts. Audits should sample claims unpredictably, so splitting one operation across a garden of accounts does not evade scrutiny; an opal or pearl can serve as a memorable label, but neither grants trust. The defense raises attack cost; it does not prove identities are unique.
